This leaves open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. We introduce MMTA (multimodal temporal analysis), a benchmark of tri-modal tasks with diverse cross-modal complementarity patterns among time series, text, and vision. MMTA spans nine domains -- robotics, autonomous driving, human action, manufacturing, AR assistance, healthcare, recommendation, finance, and climate -- under video+TS and image+TS layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split covering classification and forecasting. The benchmark standardizes heterogeneous real-world sources into a shared schema with domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics that penalize both wrong answers and failed generations. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs reveals a shared bottleneck: representing time series as text creates very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence, especially in long-video settings. We then introduce TimeOmni-v, a multimodal LLM extension with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head. TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, showing that MMTA not only exposes representation and grounding failures but also motivates targeted model design.
why: Multimodal time-series benchmark; finance one of nine domains

title: On integrability of local utility maximizing strategies
abstract: In stochastic control problems involving optimal portfolio choice, one often seeks an optimizer of some local criterion (dynamic programming value function) generated by some global criterion (e.g., expected utility). The local optimizer then typically acts as a stochastic integrand with respect to some multivariate stochastic process (e.g., asset prices). This paper takes a closer look at local criteria in the form of ``local expected utility''. Since the existence of the local optimizer can be established under very mild conditions, it is crucial to understand under what circumstances the local optimizer has good integrability properties. It is shown that the reasonable asymptotic elasticity condition of Kramkov and Schachermayer (1999) applied to the local utility function plays a key role in this context.
why: Integrability theory for utility maximization; no data

title: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions
abstract: Game-theoretic benchmarks claim that large language model (LLM) strategic decision-making varies across game types, interaction structures, and capability dimensions. However, they only evaluate strategic performance across individual fixed models. In parallel, contemporary LLM routers pick models under quality-cost trade-offs, but with no notion of a strategic structure. They do not account for an opponent that might be unknown, and that can adapt over time and shift the feedback signal. To address this, we extend the game-theoretic evaluations and define strategic selection as the meta game layered on top of the base game. In each round, a strategic selector fields an LLM from a portfolio of models to navigate a game payoff matrix that is latent and learned online. We find that the evaluation signal is game-specific, and that extracting a reliable signal requires a much higher number of seed runs $N$ compared to traditional benchmarking setups. Evaluating across 5 games and 10 LLMs, we show a model's strategic competence varies significantly depending on the game setup and the opponent faced. Building on this, we implement a suite of selector methods and find that approaches that rely on query embeddings or LLM self-reflection do not consistently capture the underlying strategic signal. A lightweight multi-armed bandit algorithm performs more reliably across games, though it still falls short of the best fixed model. Finally, we show that simple non-stationary and adversarial bandit variants fail to outperform a stationary bandit baseline, pointing to a gap in how current methods handle a shifting opponent in strategic settings.
why: LLM selection in games; not financial

title: A GLE-LSV model with state-dependent leverage and colored noise
abstract: We study a local stochastic volatility (LSV) model in which the variance factor follows a generalized Langevin equation (GLE) with colored noise, and past returns act on variance through a memory kernel with state-dependent amplitudes. For kernels given by finite sums of exponentials, we prove existence, uniqueness, and non-explosion under a growth condition linking the volatility map to the potential. In a one-mode family with a polynomial potential, feedback through log returns can cause explosion exactly when the squared volatility factor grows faster than the restoring force. Under structural and nondegeneracy conditions, an exact reduced Markovian state has a smooth density solving a deterministic forward equation. The Dupire conditional expectation therefore requires no stochastic partial differential equation. Under a bounded Sharpe ratio, exponential utility selects the minimal entropy martingale measure, whose premium solves a quadratic backward stochastic differential equation. Under a regularity hypothesis, which we verify in special cases with and without leverage, the premium depends only on the current state, and the squared VIX equals the expected average future local stochastic variance. Finally, a regularized calibration problem with bid--ask constraints admits a minimizer whenever a feasible point has finite objective value.
why: GLE stochastic volatility theory; no data or practice path.

title: The Missile and the Toll: Two-Way Flow Through the Strait of Hormuz
abstract: Tolls for safe passage and attacks on shipping are usually treated as mutually exclusive: either ships pay or attacks happen. We argue they are complementary. In a Stackelberg escalation game for the Strait of Hormuz, the enforcer chooses an attack intensity and a toll schedule; the response is to pay, cross exposed, wait, reroute, or exit. Attacks create the willingness to pay; tolls harvest it. The model predicts asymmetry across trade forms: a toll where the cargo owner can pay and the vessel owner will consent, and none where either fails. Any such payment is clandestine, but the model's implications are testable against freight rates, insurance premia, and incident reports.
why: Hormuz toll game theory; untestable here, no data

title: Is the Future Predictable? Modeling Future Predictability for Reliable Temporal Reasoning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable when reasoning about the future. Existing models often overlook the difference among future states, committing to specific answers even when the queried facts are inherently volatile. To capture this challenge, we introduce ChronoRegime, a future-oriented temporal reasoning task that requires models to determine whether historical temporal evidence justifies commitment to a future answer. Furthermore, we propose Confidence-Aware Temporal Reasoning (CTR), a framework that estimates future predictability from temporal dynamics and regulates answer commitment accordingly. Rather than performing unconditional forecasting, CTR commits only when the reconstructed evidence supports the target future state. Across multiple LLMs, CTR improves strict overall accuracy by 6.7 percentage points and reduces hallucination rates by 18.4 percentage points on average over the plain QA baseline. These results demonstrate that explicit predictability assessment is an effective mechanism for safer and more reliable temporal reasoning under future uncertainty.
why: Temporal reasoning benchmark for LLMs; no finance work.

title: Triage-PiEvo: Evidence Admission for Principle-Evolving Scientific Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based AI Scientists advance scientific discovery, yet they suffer from inefficiencies due to noisy observations. Existing principle-evolving agents act on every anomaly, leaving its source unresolved: a new mechanism or an evaluation artifact, so invalid revisions bias evolution. To address this, we formulate revision as evidence admission: anomalies steer search immediately, but only independently verified evidence may rewrite persistent principles, and contradicted principles are retracted. We realize this in TRIAGE-PIEVO , which pairs an anomaly-responsive search portfolio with a staged verification gate that alone controls what enters principle state. Across four scientific tasks with three backbones, TRIAGE-PIEVO (1) attains the highest average solution quality with +7.5%~11.8% over the strongest baseline per backbone, matching the strongest baseline's full-budget quality with one-third of the evaluation budget on Qwen3-235B; and additional stress tests and cross-harness deployment demonstrate that (2) in constructed stress tests, it admits none of the corrupted, hidden-source, or exploit evidence that ungated variants admit, while missing no planted mechanism, and (3) plugged unchanged into three external research harnesses, it cuts false evidence admissions by over 60% and raises verified scores by 31%~43%.
why: Scientific-agent search method; no finance content

title: LYNX: Analytical Program Synthesis via Grounding and Closed-Loop Refinement
abstract: LLM-powered data analytics aims to translate natural language instructions into executable analytical programs over underlying data. However, existing approaches, whether treating LLMs as intent-to-code translators or as standalone analytical engines, often fail to reliably align domain semantics with complex schemas and heterogeneous metadata, resulting in brittle execution and semantically inconsistent analytical outputs in real-world workloads. We present LYNX, a multi-agent framework that formulates LLM-driven analytics as a schema- and knowledge-constrained analysis problem rather than a single-pass generation task. LYNX organizes analytical synthesis into a closed-loop workflow of planning, generation, verification, and refinement through three role-specialized agents that collaboratively enforce schema grounding, semantic consistency, and execution correctness. To address domain ambiguity and schema misalignment, LYNX integrates Semantic-Structural Distillation and Stage-Aware Allocation (SSD-SAA). A delta-guided iterative revision continuously diagnoses and repairs semantic and execution-level failures, substantially improving synthesis robustness. We evaluate LYNX on two NL-to-SQL benchmarks, BIRD-SQL Mini-Dev and the more challenging Spider 2.0-Lite. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance and efficiency, achieving 10.66% to 59.54% execution accuracy across lightweight and commercial models, while reducing token consumption by 70.53% compared with the prior most efficient method. Our framework displays high generalization over different backbones, from open-source, lightweight models to the latest commercial models. Additional case studies on quantitative finance analytics and complex multi-relational SQL workloads further demonstrate the framework's robustness, scalability, and practical applicability in real-world analytical scenarios.
why: General data analytics agent; finance not central.

title: A Reference Architecture for Integrating Agentic AI into Enterprise Software: Responsibilities, Interactions, and Variability
abstract: Agentic AI moves generative AI applications toward systems that coordinate reasoning, enterprise context, model inference, and external actions. Integrating these capabilities into enterprise software introduces diverse architectural concerns, from orchestration, knowledge and memory, and model access to tools and actions, security, runtime infrastructure, and evaluation. Existing research and industry architectures address many of these concerns but differ in scope, abstraction, responsibility organization, interaction representation, and assumptions about which capabilities are required. This paper presents a technology-neutral reference architecture for enterprise agentic AI integration. We synthesize architectural capabilities from research publications, industry architecture guidance, and interoperability specifications by architectural purpose, organize them into ten responsibilities, and define boundary invariants, typed cross-responsibility interactions, and variation points that distinguish responsibilities from condition-dependent capabilities and replaceable realization mechanisms. We instantiate the architecture as an ESG portfolio-analysis and pre-trade compliance agent over an existing service-oriented ESG metric computation and reporting system, and complement the case with a mapping of an independently published agentic architecture. The case realizes seven of the ten responsibilities; different questions take different interaction paths, controls activate only under their conditions, and the probed boundary invariants hold. The independent architecture maps onto the proposed responsibilities without requiring an additional one. These results provide initial evidence for the architecture's organization and applicability rather than its completeness. The deployment and recorded results are available as a replication package.
why: Enterprise agent reference architecture; no finance or evaluation

title: Too Late to Prune: Generative AI, the Screen, and Team Creative Decisions
abstract: Generative AI makes options cheap and shifts the bottleneck of creative work from generating options to screening them. We argue that AI's value depends on whether its options arrive before or after the team's screen. In our model, early options compete for a place in the portfolio; late options arrive after that competition and are kept unscreened. In a preregistered experiment, we randomly assigned 148 three-person teams to five schedules of access to the same language model during a product-design task with timed search and selection stages. Moving the same 15 minutes of access from search to selection lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations, although teams used the model at similar rates. Platform logs locate the difference at the screen. Early access enlarged the pool of ideas fivefold, and teams pruned it. Late-access teams reached the screen with the same small pool as teams without AI and then searched again, devoting 29% of their selection-stage queries to generating new options, compared with 11% for teams with access throughout. Late access added breadth, not quality: these teams submitted 73% more proposals than did teams without AI. Language-model judges detected the benefit of access but not the cost of late timing.
why: Generative AI in team creativity experiment; not finance

title: Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Learning based Topology-Agnostic Defense for Virtual Power Plants
abstract: The rapid proliferation of distributed energy resources (DERs) aggregated by virtual power plants (VPPs) elevates cybersecurity risk by expanding the attack surface. A coordinated cyberattack has the potential to disrupt distribution-system, bulk-system, and market operations. Existing cyberphysical defense strategies largely assume access to grid network models and operating conditions, which may not be available to third-party aggregators. This paper proposes a novel hybrid, perturbation-based cyber-physical defense for VPP-operated DERs that blends game-theoretic planning with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) under a Bayesian belief-update framework. Topology agnosticism is defined from the VPP information and implementation perspective: the VPP does not require access to the feeder topology, line parameters, switching configuration, or full system state. This work advances the state of the art through three contributions: (1) a multi-output Gaussian process with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for discrete attacker-type inference, probability of detection, and confidence of detection for modeling the belief distribution; (2) moment-matched Gaussian propagation of posterior beliefs across episodes; and (3) an RL policy that adaptively integrates Stackelberg leader (VPP) actions with exploration. Furthermore, we establish equilibrium existence and derive an episode-level closed-loop utility bound connecting attacker-belief uncertainty with GT-RL action alignment. Evaluations on IEEE 13- and 123-Bus feeders with DER portfolios demonstrate effective detection under attacker-model uncertainty and evaluated feeder re-configuration conditions, while requiring no explicit feeder-topology knowledge. Overall, the results indicate that combining bi-level game-theoretic planning, nonparametric Bayesian inference, and adaptive RL is a promising direction for VPP cybersecurity.
why: Power-grid cyber defense; off-topic

title: Revisited Support Vector Machines: A Unified Joint Optimization Framework with Nyström Approximation for Scalable Adaptive Learning
abstract: The theoretical elegance of Support Vector Machines (SVMs), grounded in statistical learning theory, establishes them as a reference for robust classification. However, in the era of Big Data, classical SVMs face two major bottlenecks: the prohibitive cubic complexity $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ of training and the rigidity of static kernels. Traditional methodologies treat kernel selection as a discrete, "brute-force" GridSearch problem, effectively decoupling the learning of data representation from the optimization of the decision boundary. This paper proposes a paradigm shift with a so-called "Revisited SVM", a unified framework that recasts the learning process as a continuous %bi-level joint optimization problem. We derive a novel objective function $J(α, θ)$ that allows for the simultaneous optimization of dual Lagrange multipliers and kernel hyper-parameters. To solve this challenging non-convex problem efficiently, we introduce a hybrid Block Coordinate Ascent (BCA) algorithm, tightly integrated with Nyström-based low-rank approximation, which drastically reduces computational complexity to $\mathcal{O}(Nm)$. Extensive experiments conducted across four heterogeneous domains (Bioinformatics, Finance, Cybersecurity, and Computer Vision) demonstrate that our approach not only matches but often exceeds exhaustive GridSearch accuracy, while delivering training speedups of up to 100x. Notably, on the complex NSL-KDD intrusion detection dataset, our adaptive kernel approach achieves 96.25\% accuracy compared to a mere 50\% for standard baselines, proving its unique ability to model complex non-linear manifolds in high-dimensional spaces. We validate our results using rigorous statistical tests and provide a theoretical convergence analysis of the proposed algorithm.
why: Generic SVM scaling method; no finance grounding.

title: Agent-Canary-Mas: End-to-End Evaluation of Protocol Risk in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Agent-to-agent protocols allow LLM agents to discover peers, exchange results, and coordinate tool use. A locally successful protocol attack, however, may be rejected by a later agent or propagated into a consequential task decision. Measuring local exploitability alone leaves this difference unresolved and provides limited evidence about which participant caused the final outcome. We present Agent-Canary-Mas, an end-to-end evaluation system that follows protocol risk through long-horizon multi-agent tasks. It covers five risk classes and 13 subclasses across A2A, ANP, and BCS, with 975 matched malicious--benign task pairs in five business domains. A shared OpenClaw framework runs autonomous, tool-using agents under different underlying models while preserving the task and execution setup. Matched runs separate local protocol success from downstream consequences; retained evidence connects participant selection, message consumption, tool activity, and task-state changes. We further evaluate a protocol-context Guard that checks an object's authority at consequential handoffs. Across three model conditions, local attack success is frequently at or above 90%, while consequence conversion ranges from 7.1\% to 100.0\%. Cross-agent evidence raises macro-averaged Audit-F1 from 29.7% to 95.5%. On Finance tasks, the Guard lowers average ASR from 86.1% to 53.8% and PTCR from 65.5% to 31.2%, with a measurable completion tradeoff. These results show that protocol risk depends on how agents use exchanged objects throughout the task, and that evaluating this path supports more informative risk assessment, attribution, and defense.
why: Agent protocol security evaluation; off-topic

title: Asymmetric $q$-Gaussian Distributions from Tsallis Maximum Entropy
abstract: Within the framework of non-extensive statistical mechanics, $q$-Gaussian distributions arise as maximum-entropy solutions of Tsallis entropy under suitable escort moment constraints. Although widely used in physics, biology, geology, finance, and related fields, standard $q$-Gaussians are intrinsically symmetric and cannot capture asymmetric fluctuations often observed in empirical data. We ask whether asymmetry can arise from the Tsallis maximum-entropy principle without externally skewing or joining distributions. We show that this is achieved by retaining the Tsallis entropy and imposing a global escort mean together with distinct downside and upside escort semi-variances. The key step is to reformulate the problem of maximum Tsallis entropy in terms of the escort density. The nonlinear escort constraints then become affine, while maximizing Tsallis entropy becomes equivalent to maximizing a strictly concave functional over a convex feasible set. Consequently, any admissible stationary solution is the unique global maximizer of the corresponding variational problem. The finite-sample approximation properties of the proposed asymmetric $q$-Gaussian are studied through Monte Carlo experiments using synthetic data generated from Azzalini skew-Student distributions. Compared with the classical symmetric $q$-Gaussian, the asymmetric specification systematically provides a closer approximation to synthetic asymmetric heavy-tailed distributions. Finally, we fit the model to return series from major equity indices, a commodity, and cryptocurrencies, and compare its in-sample goodness of fit with that of a symmetric $q$-Gaussian. The results show that the asymmetric model offers a closer in-sample description of unconditional return distributions, most clearly in the tails.
why: Asymmetric q-Gaussian derivation; pure mathematics.

title: Dirichlet sub-mixtures: A new reading of multiplicative background risk models with Pareto margins
abstract: Multiplicative background risk models (MBRMs) provide a tractable framework for describing dependent risks. We construct a class of MBRMs with Pareto margins by combining Marshall--Olkin exponential and additive gamma risk factor structures, each allowed to incorporate idiosyncratic and systemic background risk factors. Our main result establishes, under an admissibility condition on the risk factor systems, a finite sub-mixture representation of the joint survival function in terms of Pareto survival functions, whose weights are Dirichlet probabilities of orderings induced by the background risk factors and sum to at most one. This yields a new interpretation of such MBRMs, in which dependence is expressed through Pareto survival functions and their Dirichlet weights. The resulting family encompasses many known multivariate Pareto constructions, is closed under marginalization, and admits characterizations of independence and, under a non-degeneracy condition, of its singular and absolutely continuous parts. It is associated, its covariance decomposition separates the contributions of the two risk factor structures and their interaction, and its joint tails are regularly varying along rays. The presence of asymptotic tail dependence and the decay rates of joint exceedance probabilities are governed by the gamma risk factors alone; the exponential risk factors affect only the tail constants.
why: Multivariate Pareto dependence theory; no finance data

title: Holding Agents Accountable with Verifiable Agent Insurance
abstract: While AI agents are useful for many tasks, they regularly misbehave in destructive ways, such as deleting important data. While prior work has focused on preventing such misbehavior, we consider how to recover after an agent misbehaves. We propose verifiable agent insurance (VAI), a framework for agent providers to commit financially to promises, a list of programmatically-specified policies that an agent is meant to follow. These promises are embedded in a smart contract on an immutable ledger (e.g., a blockchain) to prevent tampering, along with a monetary escrow. A user who detects a violation of committed promises can prompt a verifier to review agent execution traces, which are logged through the agent harness's shared tool-execution path, without instrumenting each tool separately. Upon verification of the violation, the agent provider's escrow funds are paid to the reporting user. We instantiate VAI as an end-to-end implementation on an Ethereum layer-2 network, and evaluate its coverage on three prominent agent benchmarks, two of which we re-annotated to obtain task-level policy-compliance labels. Currently, many agents do not emit user authorizations and security-relevant information as explicit, structured data objects -- rather, they embed the data needed to verify policy violations in natural language exchanges. Even so, VAI manages to detect violations in 42.2% of runs containing violations across three benchmarks. By augmenting agents to explicitly emit such objects, violation detection rises to 83.0% of traces. Our findings suggest that for improved auditability, agents should be co-designed with their security policies to emit explicit, structured records of user authorization and security-relevant actions.
why: Blockchain insurance for agents; not financial research.

title: Issifu AI Value Assessment Matrix An Evidence- and Trust-Based Framework for AI Investment Governance and Value Realization
abstract: Artificial Intelligence projects are often prioritized according to the value and feasibility estimates. It can overestimate opportunities that appear to be commercially viable, but have no evidence, are not operationally ready or are not ready for responsible scaling, because of trust conditions. This paper introduces I-AVAM™ (Issifu AI Value Assessment Matrix), a conceptual decision matrix to evaluate the opportunities of AI with four perspectives: Business Value, AI Readiness, Confidence, and Trust. These dimensions are linked to 6 decision mechanisms, including the Evidence Multiplier™, the Trust-to-Scale Index™, the Benefit Reliability Factor™, the Awudu Convergence Index™ (ACI™), the Scale Eligibility Index™ and Blocking Gap Logic™. Since ACI™ is geometric mean, it will not be hidden by high scores in other dimensions if the others are weak. The framework differentiates between opportunity attractiveness and evidence strength, scale permission, convergence, and realized benefit reliability. The paper discusses the framework architecture, fundamental equations, scoring logic, a sample application, research propositions and a validation agenda. I-AVAM™ is not a standard for all products to be tested; it is a base line model. It is the Awudu Convergence Principle™ that it proposes: AI investments must be accelerated when Value, Readiness, Evidence and Trust converge.
why: Conceptual governance matrix; no empirical content.

title: Beyond the Human-AI Capability Boundary: Rethinking the Purpose of Accounting Education
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how accounting work is accomplished and raising questions about how accounting education should respond. One increasingly visible response is to emphasise capabilities in which humans appear to retain comparative advantage, such as critical thinking, professional scepticism and judgement. This paper challenges human–AI comparative advantage as an organising basis for determining the purpose of accounting education. Drawing on a critical integrative review, the paper develops this argument in two stages. First, as accounting work is increasingly accomplished through combinations of human and technological contribution, the human–AI capability boundary becomes a less adequate basis for conceptualising professional capability. Second, the distribution of capability does not, by itself, determine the institutional allocation of professional responsibility. The paper therefore proposes that the purpose of accounting education should be to prepare students for knowledgeable, critical and responsible participation in professional accounting practice under changing technological conditions. On this account, educational purpose rests on preparing students to understand accounting outcomes, evaluate whether they warrant reliance, and remain accountable for their professional use, rather than on preserving capabilities that currently distinguish human from technological performance.
why: Accounting education position paper; off-topic.

title: Uncovering the Generative Landscape of Diffusion Models: A Spectral-Guided Quality-Diversity Diffusion Framework
abstract: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models have emerged as powerful generative priors across domains ranging from molecular design to high-resolution image synthesis. However, standard diffusion sampling is inherently biased toward high-likelihood regions, often limiting the diversity of outputs. In many domains, a single, high-likelihood sample is insufficient. Instead, diverse portfolios of high-performing solutions are required, motivating methods that uncover a model's full expressive range. Here we show that integrating Quality-Diversity (QD) optimisation with diffusion models enables the discovery of diverse, high-performing outputs. We first propose Quality-Diversity Diffusion, a framework that adapts QD to diffusion models by directly optimising the model's latent noise and conditioning embeddings and leveraging embedding models to quantify diversity. Second, we introduce a novel h-space Spectral Mutation operator, which guides search along directions of maximal semantic sensitivity by analysing principal singular vectors of the model's input-to-activation Jacobian. We evaluate our combined approach, Spectral-Guided Quality-Diversity Diffusion, on text-to-image generation. Against 12 baselines, our method consistently achieves the lowest FID score, demonstrating an excellent balance of image quality and diversity.
why: Diffusion quality-diversity for generative models; off-topic.

title: Hardware-Assisted Multi-Stage Ransomware Detection with Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: Ransomware is a fast-escalating privacy threat causing significant financial and data losses worldwide. As attacks grow more sophisticated, traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to defend. In this paper, we propose an novel framework that couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring to achieve efficient ransomware detection and mitigation. The contributions are threefold: (1) we employ adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation and leverage hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection; (2) we integrate neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalizability; and (3) We validate the proposed approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods. Moreover, it provides trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.
why: Ransomware detection; off-topic.

title: Learning Perceptual Geometry of Natural Odor Mixtures from LLM-Derived Descriptors
abstract: The relationship between odor chemistry and perception remains incompletely understood. Many existing studies focus on the perception of single molecules, whereas natural odors contain tens to hundreds of components, adding extra layer of complexity to percept formation. Here, we explore the relationship between molecular composition and perceived similarity in natural odor objects. We study this using a database of more than 1,200 volatile-compound-in-food mixtures containing more than 8,000 molecular components, and use large language models (LLMs) as a scalable surrogate for deriving mixture-level perceptual descriptions. We find that language-derived representations provide useful supervision for predicting held-out mixture similarities from molecular composition. The prediction was consistently strongest when perceptual targets were derived from chemosensory prompts than from other sensory prompts. Further, during the mixture-level training, we learned low-rank molecular embeddings that enabled better prediction of held-out mixture similarities than component-overlap metrics, even for mixture pairs with no shared molecules. Although no single-molecule labels were used during training, the learned molecular geometry showed significant alignment with the independent human odor-descriptor space. Finally, we explored the use of external molecular features in our mixture-similarity prediction task. These features showed modest zero-shot alignment with mixture-level perceptual similarity. They improved prediction under limited supervision but offered little additional predictive benefit with the full training set. Together, these results show that language-derived descriptions can provide scalable supervision for predicting the perceptual organization of complex natural mixtures, contributing to a quantitative understanding of how molecular composition gives rise to odor perception.
why: Odor perception with LLM descriptors; off-topic.
